q.intro.text: Rita draws segment A B and a point M on it, then starts a proof with the line: A M equals M B. Every line of a proof needs a reason. What may she write in the reason column? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: A first real proof, in four steps. The picture moves first, then the line and its reason.

e.step0.text: Given: A, B, C, D lie on a line in that order, and A C equals B D. Prove: A B equals C D. Line one is the given itself, with the reason: given. The drawing may show the order of the points, nothing more.

e.step1.text: Split each whole. B is between A and C, so A C equals A B plus B C. C is between B and D, so B D equals B C plus C D. Both lines cite the segment addition postulate: a starting statement of the course.

e.step2.text: A C and B D are equal, and each one equals a sum. Put the sums in their places: A B plus B C equals B C plus C D. The reason is the substitution property of equality.

e.step3.text: Both sides share B C. Take it away from both: A B equals C D, by the subtraction property of equality. Now the ticks on A B and C D are earned: every line has a reason, and none of them is: it looks that way.

e.why.text: Quick check: A B and C D looked equal from the start. Why not write A B equals C D in line one?

e.why.ok.text: Right: a drawing may show how points lie, not sizes. Only givens, markings and accepted statements count.

e.why.look.text: An accurate looking drawing can still be off, and the next one may look different. Looks are never a reason.

e.why.circ.text: That is what we are proving. Writing it first would assume the answer: that is circular.

t.intro.text: Your turn: the vertical angles, angle one and angle three. Given: angle one and angle two, and angle two and angle three, are linear pairs. Prove: angle one is congruent to angle three. Lines one and two are written for you.

t.r3.text: Line three puts the two sums in each other’s place. Which reason fits?

t.r3.ok.text: Right: both sums equal one hundred eighty degrees, so they equal each other.

t.r3.circ.text: That is the theorem we are proving. It cannot be a reason inside its own proof.

t.r3.add.text: Nothing was added to both sides. The two sums were put in each other’s place.

t.s4.text: Line four uses the subtraction property: take the measure of angle two away from both sides. Which statement is line four?

t.s4.ok.text: Right: the measure of angle two leaves both sides.

t.s4.fig.text: Close, but angle one is the angle itself, a figure. Numbers are equal: the measure of angle one equals the measure of angle three.

t.s4.side.text: The measure of angle two has to leave both sides, not one.

t.r5.text: Line five turns equal measures into congruent angles. Which reason?

t.r5.ok.text: Right: congruent angles are angles with equal measures. A definition works both ways.

t.r5.circ.text: Still circular: that theorem is what this proof establishes.

t.r5.lp.text: The linear pair postulate gives a sum of one hundred eighty degrees, not congruence.

t.status.text: Every line has a reason. Before this proof, vertical angles are congruent was something you had measured. What is it now?

t.status.ok.text: Right: a theorem, the vertical angles theorem. Watch: any crossing, the same proof.

t.status.conj.text: It was a conjecture while it was only measured. A proof from accepted statements makes it a theorem.

t.status.post.text: A postulate is accepted without proof. This one now has a proof: a theorem.

q.cb.look.text: Back to Rita: you picked, it looks that way. A drawing can show where M is on the line, never that A M equals M B.

q.cb.measure.text: Back to Rita: you picked measuring. A ruler checks one drawing, roughly. A reason has to hold for every figure that meets the givens.

q.cb.none.text: Back to Rita: you were right. With no given and no marking, nothing licenses A M equals M B. A given like, M is the midpoint, would: then the reason is the definition of midpoint.

p.intro.text: Kai measured angle three and angle six in five drawings of parallel lines cut by a transversal. Every time they matched. Kai says: alternate interior angles are congruent: proved. Is it proved?

p.build.text: Not yet: five drawings are five examples. Build the proof. First tap the lines in an order that works, two are decoys, then pick a reason for each.

p.build-test.text: Five drawings are five examples, and the next drawing could differ. Build the real proof: first tap the lines in an order that works, two are decoys, then pick a reason for each.

p.order-done.text: The order works: every line comes after what it uses. Now the reasons, top to bottom.

p.done.text: Proved: from parallel lines, the corresponding angles postulate and the vertical angles theorem, angle three and angle six are equal for every transversal. That is the alternate interior angles theorem.

p.wrong.text: Not that one: read the feedback under the proof.
